Compiled source saved at temp/handbooks/mn/notary.txt. CLASSIFICATION: Minnesota is confirmed application-only for the base notary commission -- there is NO proctored or administered exam anywhere in the fetched text of chapter 359 (Notaries Public) or chapter 358 sections 358.51-358.76 (the Revised Uniform Law on Notarial Acts, adopted 2018 c 176, effective Jan. 1, 2019). There is also NO mandatory pre-commission training or education course requirement (a targeted search of both chapters for exam/examination/course of study/training/education turned up only: a 358.14 reference to spousal 'examination' that is unrelated to notary licensing, and the RON course-of-study reference addressed below). This product is framed accordingly as a self-study/reference practice-question set grounded in real state notary law, not 'exam prep.' NOTABLE FINDING -- NO SURETY BOND: unlike most states in this application-only batch, Minnesota imposes NO surety bond requirement and NO errors-and-omissions insurance requirement anywhere in chapters 358 or 359 for the base commission or for remote online notarization. The only 'bond' reference found in either chapter is the generic catch-all in 358.11 ('if the person taking such oath be also required to give bond, the oath shall be attached to or endorsed upon such bond') -- a general rule for OTHER officeholders who may owe a bond under separate law, not a notary-specific bond mandate. This was independently verified, not assumed from other states. STATUTE STRUCTURE: Minnesota notary law is split across two chapters rather than one -- chapter 359 (12 operative sections: commission, term, stamp/register, powers, record of commission, non-English advertising notice, notary in a detached county, change of name/address, misconduct, standards of conduct, accommodation of physical limitations, taking depositions) and chapter 358 (which contains both the 26-section Revised Uniform Law on Notarial Acts at 358.51-358.76, covering definitions, authority, identification standards, certificates/short forms, interstate/tribal/federal/foreign recognition, remote online notarization, electronic-document recording, and discipline; plus roughly 10 general 'seals, oaths, acknowledgments' sections that are directly notary-relevant, including 358.15 ex officio notary public, 358.03 seal form, 358.09-358.11 oath administration/filing, 358.14 married persons, 358.115 unsworn foreign declarations, 358.116 court documents, 358.25 corporate-officer acknowledgment carve-out, and 358.50 effect of acknowledgment). Combined, roughly 48 operative sections were used as citable grounding -- a genuinely substantial, non-thin body of law once both chapters are combined, contrary to the tentative pre-research $0.50 'genuinely thinnest' slotting. NOTABLE QUIRKS DOCUMENTED IN THIS TRACK: (1) Minnesota notaries are appointed and commissioned by the GOVERNOR, with the advice and consent of the senate (359.01, subd. 1) -- the secretary of state administers applications/the register/reappointments (and may itself be designated as an agent for nonresident notaries), but appointment authority itself sits with the governor, an unusual structure compared to the secretary-of-state-appointment model used in many other states. (2) A $120 nonrefundable application fee applies (359.01, subd. 3(a)). (3) Nonresident notary appointment is narrowly limited to residents of Wisconsin, Iowa, North Dakota, or South Dakota who designate the secretary of state as agent for service of process and designate a Minnesota county of record (359.01, subd. 2). (4) Commission term runs until January 31 of the FIFTH year following the year of issuance (359.02), a somewhat unusual date-based (rather than anniversary-based) term rule, renewable up to six months early. (5) Discipline authority is split: the SECRETARY OF STATE commissions/registers notaries, while the COMMISSIONER OF COMMERCE (not the secretary of state) holds all removal/discipline power under 358.70, and a notary removed specifically by the commissioner of commerce must surrender the stamp to the commissioner (358.70, subd. 5) -- a carve-out from the general rule that the stamp is the notary's own exempt personal property (359.03, subd. 1). (6) Minnesota has a genuinely rich, clearly-labeled separate Remote Online Notarization (RON) sub-module at 358.645 (14 subdivisions) -- following the same 'separate registration on top of the base commission' pattern seen in this batch's Kansas and South Carolina tracks, though Minnesota's RON module has NO separate exam (only a separate secretary-of-state registration and technology certification). RON in Minnesota includes detailed knowledge-based-authentication identity-proofing standards (5+ questions, 5+ choices each, 2-minute limit, 80 percent passing threshold, one retry with at most 3 repeated questions), a 10-year electronic-journal/recording retention requirement, and a fee cap of $25 that -- notably -- by its own statutory text only applied to acts occurring BEFORE January 1, 2023, meaning the cap has since lapsed. The RON course-of-study reference in 358.645, subd. 13 requires the secretary of state to maintain a LIST of course providers but does not make course completion a mandatory registration prerequisite -- confirmed by close reading, not assumed. (7) Minnesota separately allows a notary to certify a printed paper copy of an electronically-signed document as a true and correct copy for county recording purposes (358.646), with its own detailed procedural requirements (personally print or supervise printing; no modifications beyond the certification) -- a distinctive authority not found in every state's notary law. (8) Ex officio notary powers are granted to four distinct categories with different scopes: legislators (no fee allowed), town/city clerks, county recorders/auditors/court commissioners (limited to their own county), and licensed peace officers (limited solely to administering oaths on probable-cause information under the Rules of Criminal Procedure) (358.15).
